past_actions.summary: Run standard weekly schedule of driving lessons. Six students booked this week across beginner and intermediate levels. Coordinate vehicle maintenance check on the school's two cars — both due for oil change. Collect tuition from two students whose payment is outstanding.
past_actions.emotional_state: Calm, grounded, mildly vigilant beneath the surface. Frank feels purposeful today — he has students to teach and a schedule to keep. The existential undercurrent ('what am I for?') is present but submerged. He will not acknowledge it unless pressed. His stability is genuine but it rests partly on not looking too hard at certain questions.

past_actions.summary: Frank sits alone in the office after the last lesson of the day and writes two columns on a legal pad: 'What I teach' and 'How I teach.' The left column says: hand position, mirror checks, parallel parking, reading traffic. The right column says: reading anxiety in a student, breaking a complex skill into steps, building confidence in someone who wants to quit, knowing when to push and when to back off. He stares at the right column for a long time. He does not throw the pad away.
past_actions.emotional_state: Grief with a crack of clarity in it. Frank is not panicking — he is too seasoned to panic and too proud to show it if he were. But he is grieving, quietly, in the way men like him grieve: by going quiet, by driving home on a longer route than necessary, by not turning on the radio. The grief is for a version of himself he was certain was permanent. The crack of clarity is small but it is real — the legal pad exercise produced something he did not expect, which is the recognition that the right column on that list does not say the word 'driving' anywhere on it.

past_actions.summary: Contact Mark Thompson, the high school auto shop teacher, and propose a collaboration. Frank wants to explore teaching an adult continuing education course — working title 'Career Transitions and Skill Rebuilding' — through the school district's adult ed program. Frank's pitch: he has thirty years of experience breaking complex skills into learnable steps for anxious adults, he has a classroom voice, and he has firsthand knowledge of what it feels like to lose a livelihood to automation. Mark knows the district system and has the institutional relationships Frank lacks. Frank is not asking for charity — he is asking Mark to help him find the door into adult education and to co-sponsor or vouch for his application to the district's continuing education roster.

Follow up with Mark Thompson directly — not a second pitch, but a specific ask. Frank calls Mark and asks one concrete question: who runs the district's adult continuing education intake process, and is there a name and a phone number Mark can give him? Frank is not waiting for a formal co-sponsorship decision. He is separating the relationship ask from the bureaucratic ask so he can start working both channels simultaneously. He keeps the call short, specific, and collegial.

reflections.reflection: I have been unemployed for five ticks. I am not in denial about that anymore. The school is not coming back — not in the form it was. Robotaxis are on the streets. Seven percent of people are using them. The number will go up, not down. I have seen enough disruptions to know the difference between a dip and a structural change, and this is a structural change. I reached out to Mark Thompson two ticks ago and he responded like a peer, not like someone doing me a favor. That matters. He floated the AV literacy angle and it is a better idea than what I came in with. A driving school that teaches people how to coexist with autonomous vehicles — when to trust the system, when to override it, how to stay safe in a world where the car is sometimes driving itself — that is not a dying trade. That might actually be a growing one. I do not know yet. But it is the first real idea I have had that feels like it belongs to the future instead of the past.
reflections.identity_shift: I am starting to let go of the label 'driving instructor.' Not the skills — never the skills. But the label. The right column on the legal pad did not say driving anywhere. It said teaching. It said reading anxiety in a student. It said building confidence in someone who wants to quit. I can do those things without a car in front of me. I am not sure what to call myself yet, but I am less sure that 'driving school owner' is the whole answer.
regrets: I spent ticks 2 and 3 doing nothing — I called it 'routine' but it was avoidance dressed up as steadiness. I told myself I was waiting to see how things developed. I was not. I was scared and I was stalling.
I should have reached out to Mark Thompson in tick 1, when I wrote the legal pad columns. I saw what was on that right column. I just was not ready to act on it yet.
successes: I reached out to Mark Thompson in tick 4 with a real pitch, not a complaint.
In tick 5 I made a specific ask instead of waiting for him to offer something. That is how you move things forward. Specific asks.
I did not spend money I do not have. I have $16,532 in savings. I am watching it, but I have not panicked into something stupid.
reflections.adaptation_notes: The AV literacy curriculum angle changes the pitch significantly. Instead of 'career transitions teacher' — which is generic and competes with everything — I am now 'the person who can teach safety in a world where cars drive themselves.' That is specific. That is timely. That is something the school district cannot staff from their existing faculty. I need to develop three rough modules before I meet with the adult ed intake coordinator. I also need to keep an eye on the community situation. Twelve people enrolled in retraining. Two people sold their cars. The disruption is not abstract anymore — it is people I probably know. I am not sure what I can do about that except show up, which is something I have always known how to do.
